passage: I'm Payal, and I watched my little sister Indu's sports day from the stands. The teacher handed out bibs from a basket without looking: red or yellow. Indu got yellow. Two minutes later she was jumping up and down, shouting, "Yellow is the best! Yellow is the fastest!" Her friend Moti got red, and Indu stuck her tongue out. They had shared a tiffin that very morning. In the tug-of-war the yellows chanted, "Red is slow!" Indu screamed loudest. Afterwards she told me, very seriously, "Yellow people are better." Nobody had chosen anything. The bibs came out of a basket.

qa.q: How were the bibs handed out?
qa.a: From a basket without looking.

qa.q: What does Indu's 'Yellow people are better' suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt proud and attached to her team, as if being yellow made her part of something better.

qa.q: What could the teacher try next sports day so the fun of teams doesn't turn into teasing?
qa.a: Mix the bibs between races and cheer both colours, so children enjoy belonging without looking down on the other side.

qa.q: What might Moti feel when Indu sticks her tongue out, after they shared a tiffin that morning?
qa.a: Moti may feel hurt and confused that a friend turned against Moti just because of a bib.

grounding: An older sister watches a five-year-old cheer her randomly assigned colour as the best and tease a friend on the other team.

passage: Monday. Anjali Miss handed out bibs from a box without looking: green or blue. Elizabeth, five, got green and hugged her bib like a present. Wednesday. At the races Elizabeth shouted, "Green wins! Blue is babies!" The greens laughed and held hands. The blue children frowned. Friday. Anjali Miss said, "New week, new teams," and gave out bibs again. Elizabeth got blue. For a moment she looked stricken. Then she pulled it on, ran to the blue side and shouted, "Blue is the best!" Anjali Miss hid a smile.

qa.q: What colour did Elizabeth get on Friday?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when she first got a green bib?
qa.a: She was delighted and proud, hugging it like a present.

qa.q: Why was Anjali Miss's choice to change teams on Friday a good one?
qa.a: It showed the children that teams are just bibs from a box, so 'blue is babies' can't stick to anyone.

qa.q: How might the blue children have felt on Wednesday?
qa.a: They likely felt teased and cross, being called babies for a colour they didn't choose.

grounding: A five-year-old given a random bib quickly decides her colour is best and teases the other side, then does the same for her new colour.

passage: Rain drove sports hour into the small school hall, where the floor was slippery. Miss tied red ribbons on half the class and blue on the rest, just by where they sat. Charu, six, got red. Her best friend Lavanya got blue. "Red team! Red team!" Charu chanted. By the second game she wouldn't pass the beanbag to Lavanya. "You're blue. Blue people cheat." Lavanya's lip wobbled. "I'm not a cheater. I'm Lavanya." Charu stopped, beanbag in hand. Miss called, "Everyone into a circle, reds and blues mixed." Charu sat down next to Lavanya, unsure, still holding her red ribbon.

qa.q: Where did sports hour take place because of the rain?
qa.a: In the small school hall.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she stopped with the beanbag in her hand?
qa.a: She seemed unsure, caught by Lavanya's words and realising her friend was not a 'blue cheater'.

qa.q: What choice did Miss make, and why might it help?
qa.a: Miss had everyone sit in a mixed circle, reminding them that reds and blues are all one class.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's 'I'm not a cheater. I'm Lavanya' show about how Lavanya felt?
qa.a: Lavanya felt hurt at being treated as just 'blue' and wanted to be seen as a friend again.

grounding: A six-year-old handed a random ribbon quickly sees her team as better and turns on her best friend in the other colour.

subtype: Pride in the group and dislike of rivals [Actor]
passage: Dear Diary, Our house, Kaveri, lost the inter-house quiz to Ganga by one point. ONE point. It felt like a punch in the stomach, even though I wasn't on the quiz team. At lunch the Kaveri lot started chanting, "Ganga cheated, Ganga cheated," and I joined in loudest. Avni, who is in Ganga and sits next to me, went red and stopped talking to me. I didn't care then. Now it's night, and I keep thinking about it. Avni lent me her geometry box on Monday. She didn't cheat. The quiz master was a Kaveri teacher! I think I was just sad, and it came out mean. Tomorrow I'll say sorry. I'm still proud of Kaveri, though. - Jomon

qa.q: By how many points did Kaveri lose the quiz?
qa.a: By one point.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel when Kaveri lost?
qa.a: It felt like a punch in the stomach to Jomon, a personal hurt even without being on the quiz team.

qa.q: What choice has Jomon made for tomorrow, and why does it matter?
qa.a: To say sorry to Avni, because the chant was sadness coming out as meanness toward a friend who hadn't cheated.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Avni during the chant?
qa.a: Avni went red and stopped talking, hurt at being called a cheater by the classmate she sits beside.

grounding: A child proud of their school house feels the loss personally and joins in mocking the rivals, then regrets hurting a friend.

subtype: Pride in the group and dislike of rivals [Actor]
passage: Every harvest season, Pranav's village played the next village at cricket on the dry paddy field. Pranav, eleven, painted his cheeks with the village's orange and yelled himself hoarse. This year the other village won by two wickets. Pranav's throat went tight. It felt as if they had beaten him personally. On the bullock-cart ride home he saw Vidya, a girl from the other village who came to his school, waving her team's green flag. "Your team plays like old buffaloes!" he shouted. The boys around him laughed. Vidya's flag dropped. Pranav felt a hot thrill, then something heavier. Vidya helped him with sums every week. He looked away and didn't shout again.

qa.q: By how many wickets did the other village win?
qa.a: By two wickets.

qa.q: What did Pranav feel after shouting at Vidya?
qa.a: First a hot thrill, then something heavier, like guilt, remembering she helps him with sums every week.

qa.q: What could Pranav do the next time his team loses?
qa.a: He could cheer his team's effort or congratulate the winners instead of mocking them, keeping his pride without turning on people like Vidya.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel when her flag dropped?
qa.a: Vidya likely felt embarrassed and hurt, mocked in front of the boys by a classmate she helps.

grounding: A village boy feels his team's loss as a personal defeat and mocks a rival supporter, a friend, before feeling the weight of it.

subtype: Pride in the group and dislike of rivals [Actor]
passage: Priscila, nine, wore her school's blue scarf to every futsal match in their Lisbon neighbourhood, even in summer. When her team lost the final to the school across the park, she cried on the bus and refused dinner. Next morning at the bakery she saw Jana from the other school, in a red scarf. Priscila's cousin whispered, "Look, a red. Tell her she lost." Priscila said loudly, "Red smells like old socks." Jana's face fell. She was only buying bread for her grandmother. Priscila felt the pride and the hurt twist together into something she didn't like. At school she asked her teacher, "Is it bad to love your team?" "No," said Ms Costa. "It's bad to hate the other one."

qa.q: What was Jana buying at the bakery?
qa.a: Bread for her grandmother.

qa.q: What did Priscila feel after the remark about old socks?
qa.a: Her pride and hurt twisted into something she didn't like, a kind of guilt.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Priscila, and what did Ms Costa's answer help her see?
qa.a: Seeing Jana's face fall; Ms Costa helped her see she can love her team without hating the other.

qa.q: How might Jana feel being mocked while buying bread?
qa.a: Jana probably felt hurt and targeted just for wearing a red scarf on an ordinary errand.

grounding: A girl proud of her school team feels its defeat deeply and mocks a rival supporter, then wonders where team love turns into dislike.

passage: Parveen Khala smiled at her nephew. "Ujjwal, you think you're the first to sulk when your team loses? When I was fifteen, our girls' school was famous for its hockey team. When we won, I walked taller, as if I had scored every goal myself. When we lost the district final, I didn't eat for a day. Then a cousin from another school laughed and said our team was all show. I shouted at her so hard that my Ammi sent me to my room. It felt as if she had insulted me, not a team. Years later I understood: my whole mood lived inside that team. So when your side loses and you feel insulted, check how much of yourself you've handed over."

qa.q: What was Parveen's school famous for?
qa.a: Its hockey team.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel when the cousin laughed at her team?
qa.a: She felt personally insulted, as if the cousin had mocked her rather than just a team.

qa.q: What does Parveen Khala suggest Ujjwal do, and why?
qa.a: To notice how much of himself he has handed over to his team, since she once let her whole mood live inside hers.

qa.q: How might the cousin have seen Parveen's shouting?
qa.a: The cousin may have been taken aback, having meant a light jab about a team, not about Parveen.

grounding: An aunt recalls how as a teenager her mood rose and fell with her school team and an insult to it felt like an insult to her.

passage: Nilesh had a maths exam at nine the next morning and his phone was at eight per cent, but he couldn't put it down. Someone had posted a mocking clip about the band he loved, and Tarun, his own friend, had commented, "Overrated, honestly." Nilesh typed a long reply, deleted it, typed a longer one. His chest was tight, as if Tarun had called him overrated. Last week, when the band won an award, Nilesh had grinned for two days as if he'd won it himself. Now the phone died mid-sentence. In the dark, Nilesh realised he'd done no revision and was furious with a friend over songs. At breakfast Tarun messaged, "Bro you ok? It was just a joke." Nilesh stared at the screen, still stung.

qa.q: What time was Nilesh's maths exam?
qa.a: At nine the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh's chest feel tight at Tarun's comment?
qa.a: He felt as if Tarun had called him overrated, because his sense of worth was tied to the band.

qa.q: What could Nilesh try the next time a comment about the band stings?
qa.a: He could put the phone down, remind himself a joke about the band isn't a verdict on him, and talk to Tarun calmly later.

qa.q: How does Tarun seem to see the comment?
qa.a: Tarun sees it as just a joke and seems surprised, checking whether Nilesh is okay.

grounding: A teenager whose mood rises and falls with a band's fortunes feels a friend's criticism of it as a personal insult, even on the night before an exam.

passage: Ujjwal's school had won the city quiz three years running, and he wore the badge on his blazer every day. On Saturday they lost to a school from across town. By Monday Ujjwal was snapping at everyone. When Parveen from the next section said, "Maybe your team got a bit lazy," Ujjwal flushed. "You don't even know what you're talking about," he said, loud enough to stop the corridor. At home he skipped dinner. His mother found him scrolling through old winning photos. "You weren't even on the team, beta." "It's still us," he said. "When they lose, it's like I lost." His mother sat beside him. "And when the school wins, are you a better boy?" Ujjwal didn't answer.

qa.q: How many years running had Ujjwal's school won the city quiz?
qa.a: Three years running.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal mean by 'When they lose, it's like I lost'?
qa.a: His own sense of worth rises and falls with the school's results, so the team's defeat feels personal.

qa.q: What question from his mother could become a turning point, and why?
qa.a: 'When the school wins, are you a better boy?', because it invites Ujjwal to separate his worth from the school's record.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when Ujjwal snapped in the corridor?
qa.a: Parveen likely felt embarrassed and surprised at such a strong reaction to a passing comment about the team.

grounding: A teenage boy's mood crashes when his school loses and he defends it fiercely, treating criticism of the team as criticism of him.

passage: I'm Darshan, and I only noticed this last term. In the hostel mess in Pune, when someone made a joke about Biharis, I suddenly felt very Bihari, more than I ever had back in Patna. In the lab, arguing about circuit design with Madhav, I was just an engineer; nobody's hometown mattered. And on match nights in the common room I was a cricket fan, yelling at the screen with guys from five states. Same week, same me, three different people stepping forward depending on who was around. At first it confused me. Then it helped. When the mess joke stung, I remembered I'm also the boy who fixed Madhav's circuit, and the one who predicted Sunday's batting collapse. No single label gets to be the whole of me.

qa.q: Whose circuit did Darshan fix?
qa.a: Madhav's circuit.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel when someone in the mess joked about Biharis?
qa.a: He suddenly felt very Bihari, more than he ever had at home, and the joke stung.

qa.q: What helped Darshan when the mess joke stung, and why?
qa.a: Remembering he is also an engineer and a cricket fan, so no single label could take over his sense of himself.

qa.q: How might Madhav see Darshan in the lab?
qa.a: Madhav likely sees Darshan simply as a fellow engineer to argue circuit design with, not by his hometown.

grounding: A student notices his regional, professional and fan identities come forward in different settings, and that seeing this stops one label from taking over.

passage: College counsellor's note, 7 March. Written by Kashish. Avni, nineteen, came in upset after a clash in a group project. She said that in her Gujarati cultural society she is proud to be "the Gujarati girl," in the coding club she is "the only woman who stays till midnight," and in her dance troupe she is just "Avni who's always late." This week a teammate joked that girls in tech "just do the slides," and for two days she felt like nothing but the woman in tech, and angry. We talked about how different parts of her take the lead depending on the company she is in. She listed five identities on a sheet. By the end she was smiling a little: "He saw one of me. There are four others." She will raise the remark with the project lead, and see me again next week.

qa.q: How many identities did Avni list on the sheet?
qa.a: Five identities.

qa.q: What does Avni's 'He saw one of me. There are four others' suggest she now feels?
qa.a: She feels less trapped by the teammate's remark, seeing it touched only one part of who she is.

qa.q: What next steps did Avni and Kashish agree on?
qa.a: Avni will raise the remark with the project lead and see Kashish again next week.

qa.q: How might Avni's dance troupe see her, compared with the coding club?
qa.a: The troupe knows her as 'Avni who's always late', a light everyday identity, while the club sees her as the woman who stays till midnight.

grounding: A student learns that different identities come forward in different settings and that recognising this keeps one label from taking over after a hurtful remark.

passage: Sunday night. Strange week. At the Delhi university welcome, everyone called me "the Bombay girl," and I found myself defending vada pav as if my life depended on it. Tuesday, in the philosophy seminar, I was only a student fighting about free will; nobody cared where I came from. Thursday, at the badminton club, I was just Ira who smashes too hard. Friday, Pema from Gangtok and I sat on the hostel roof, and she said she felt more "northeastern" in Delhi than she ever did at home. Me too, with Mumbai. It's as if different parts of me step forward depending on who's in the room. Honestly, that's a relief. If someone squeezes me down to "the Bombay girl," I know it's one door, not the house. - Ira

qa.q: What did everyone call Ira at the welcome?
qa.a: "the Bombay girl"

qa.q: Why does Ira find the week a relief?
qa.a: She realises different parts of her step forward in different rooms, so no single label can reduce her.

qa.q: How could Ira use this idea the next time someone reduces her to one label?
qa.a: She could remind herself it's 'one door, not the house' and bring forward her other sides, like student or badminton player.

qa.q: What does Pema's comment on the roof show about Pema's experience?
qa.a: Pema also feels a regional identity grow stronger away from home, feeling more 'northeastern' in Delhi than in Gangtok.

grounding: A student notices her regional, academic and sporting identities come forward in different settings, and that seeing this stops one label from taking over.

passage: The panel had twenty minutes to choose between two final candidates, and the manager was already late for a flight. Mahima, twenty-five, noticed her pen hovering over the first name: a graduate of her own college, whose professors she knew and whose jokes she'd laughed at. The other, Sharmila, came from the rival college whose students had booed Mahima's team at every fest. Mahima felt the tug, warm and familiar. She put the pen down. "Let me check the scores again," she said. On the case exercise, Sharmila was stronger by a clear margin. Mahima reminded herself they would all be on one team now: same city office, same clients. "Sharmila," she said. The manager nodded and left for the airport. Walking back, Mahima still felt proud of her old college. It just didn't get to choose for her.

qa.q: How long did the panel have to choose?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Mahima feel when her pen hovered over the first name?
qa.a: She felt a warm, familiar tug to favour a graduate of her own college.

qa.q: What choice did Mahima make, and what helped her make it fairly?
qa.a: She rechecked the scores and chose Sharmila, reminding herself they would all be on one team, in the same office, with the same clients.

qa.q: How would things have changed for Sharmila if Mahima had followed the tug?
qa.a: Sharmila, the stronger candidate, would have lost the job because of an old college rivalry rather than her work.

grounding: A young panellist notices the pull to favour her own college, turns to the wider shared identity of one team, and judges an outsider fairly while keeping her pride.

passage: The two blocks of the Hebbal apartment complex had never got along: Block A said Block B's kids were rough, Block B said A's were spoilt. Vishal, twenty-six and the new father of a toddler, caught himself nodding along at an A-block meeting. Then one evening at the park his daughter tripped, and it was Usha from Block B who scooped her up and dusted her knees before he could get there. Usha's son had the same scab on the same knee. They both laughed. Sitting on the bench, Vishal realised they were just two tired parents in the same park. At the next A-block meeting, when someone said, "B people never pay maintenance on time," Vishal said, "Let's check the records before we say that." He suggested a joint parents' group for the play area. Some grumbled. Twelve families joined.

qa.q: Who scooped up Vishal's daughter when she tripped?
qa.a: Usha from Block B.

qa.q: What did Vishal realise on the bench with Usha?
qa.a: That they were just two tired parents in the same park, not rivals from different blocks.

qa.q: What choices did Vishal make at the next A-block meeting?
qa.a: He asked to check the records before blaming B people, and suggested a joint parents' group for the play area.

qa.q: How might Usha see Block A after this?
qa.a: Usha may feel the divide soften, having been treated as a fellow parent rather than as one of the 'B people'.

grounding: A young father notices his pull toward his own block, finds a wider shared identity as a parent, and pushes for fairness toward the other block.

passage: "Papa, the Menons want to rent the upstairs flat." Bhupen frowned over his newspaper. "Menons? Not from here. Better to give it to someone from our own people." Sabina put down her tea. "Papa, when you came to Guwahati for your job, weren't you 'not from here' too?" "That was different." "How?" "We... fitted in." "Because Mr Barua's family gave you a chance. You've told me that story a hundred times." Bhupen was silent. "Mr Menon teaches at my college. They have a baby. They've paid the deposit on time for every flat they've rented." "And if they're noisy?" "Then we talk to them, same as we'd talk to anyone." Bhupen folded the paper slowly. "Call them for tea on Sunday. Both families."

qa.q: Where does Mr Menon teach?
qa.a: At Sabina's college.

qa.q: What does Bhupen's silence after Sabina's reminder suggest?
qa.a: He seems to recognise that he was once an outsider given a chance, and that his objection doesn't hold up.

qa.q: Which of Sabina's arguments changed Bhupen's mind, and why?
qa.a: Reminding him that Mr Barua's family gave him a chance when he was new, which widened 'our own people' to anyone who once needed a start.

qa.q: What would change for the Menons if Bhupen had refused?
qa.a: The Menons, a family with a baby and a good record, would lose a home simply for not being 'from here'.

grounding: A young woman helps her father move past favouring 'our own people' by recalling a wider shared identity as newcomers, so an outsider family is treated fairly.

subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
passage: Pallavi Nani pulled her grandson onto the swing beside her. "Uday, you're upset because Rishi has a new phone? When I was nine, my friend Kamla got a red bicycle with a bell and a basket. I had my brother's old cycle, which worked perfectly, and shoes, and three meals, and a mother who plaited my hair every morning. But when I saw that red bicycle, I went home and cried into my pillow. I told my mother we were poor. She laughed and said, 'Poor? Count what's on this table.' I didn't want to count. I wanted red. For a whole week I hated my old cycle, though nothing about it had changed. Only what I was looking at had changed."

qa.q: What colour was Kamla's new bicycle?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi cry into her pillow?
qa.a: Seeing Kamla's red bicycle made her feel poor by comparison, even though she had everything she needed.

qa.q: What did Pallavi's mother suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: To count what was on the table, turning Pallavi's eyes from the bicycle to what she actually had.

qa.q: What might Uday take from Nani's story about Rishi's phone?
qa.a: Uday may see that the sadness comes from comparing with Rishi, not from actually lacking anything.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how as a child with enough at home she felt poor and sad after seeing a friend's new bicycle, because of comparison, not lack.

subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
passage: It was half-yearly exam week, and Indu, ten, was supposed to be revising fractions. Instead she kept thinking about Payal's new phone, shiny and pink, which Payal had shown the whole bench that morning, along with photos of her new bicycle. Indu had a bicycle too, Didi's old blue one, and a home with plenty of dal and books and a grandmother who told stories. None of that seemed to count now. At dinner she pushed her rice around. "Why can't we have nice things?" Ma looked up from the electricity bill. "Is something missing, Indu?" Indu opened her mouth, then closed it. Nothing was missing. Payal's things were just newer. She went back to fractions, still heavy, and a little ashamed of feeling it.

qa.q: What colour was Payal's new phone?
qa.a: Pink.

qa.q: Why did Indu feel ashamed as well as heavy?
qa.a: She realised nothing was actually missing at home; her sadness came only from comparing with Payal's newer things.

qa.q: What question did Ma ask, and how did it help Indu?
qa.a: 'Is something missing, Indu?', which made Indu notice she had enough and that the hurt came from comparison.

qa.q: How might Ma feel hearing 'Why can't we have nice things?' while looking at the electricity bill?
qa.a: Ma might feel a pang of hurt or worry, since the family provides plenty and yet her daughter feels poor.

grounding: A girl with enough at home feels sad after seeing a classmate's new phone and bicycle, and realises the hurt comes from comparison, not lack.

subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
passage: In their Hyderabad colony, Sumit came down on Sunday on a brand-new geared bicycle, a phone in his pocket "for emergencies." The other children crowded round. Mridul, eight, stood at the edge with his old cycle, the one with a squeaky pedal that Papa oiled every week. Yesterday he had loved it. Today it looked small and ugly. He went home and lay on the sofa. "What happened, Mridul?" asked his mother. "Nothing." "You have a face like a burst balloon." "Sumit has everything, and I have nothing," he muttered. His mother looked around the room: his books, his cricket bat, his fish tank. "Nothing?" Mridul looked too. He didn't answer, but he stopped kicking the cushion.

qa.q: What did Papa oil every week?
qa.a: The squeaky pedal on Mridul's old cycle.

qa.q: Why did Mridul's cycle look small and ugly today when he had loved it yesterday?
qa.a: Seeing Sumit's new geared bicycle made his own seem worse, though nothing about his cycle had changed.

qa.q: What choice did Mridul's mother make, and why did it help?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, she looked round at his books, bat and fish tank and asked 'Nothing?', letting him see what he has.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel if he knew Mridul had gone home upset?
qa.a: Sumit might be surprised, having only shown off a new bicycle without meaning to make anyone sad.

grounding: A boy who has enough feels he has nothing after seeing a friend's new bicycle and phone, until his mother helps him see the hurt comes from comparison.

passage: Sofia had got a B-plus in chemistry, the best grade she'd ever had at her school in Madrid. She was proud for exactly ten minutes, until Layla, at the next desk, got an A-minus. Layla always seemed one step ahead: slightly better grades, slightly newer trainers, a family that went to the coast every August while Sofia's family went to her grandparents' village. Sofia felt cheated, as if something had been taken from her. On the metro home she scrolled through Layla's holiday photos and felt worse. Then she remembered that a year ago she had failed chemistry. And last summer in the village she had laughed more than in any summer before. Her B-plus hadn't changed. Only the person she was measuring against had.

qa.q: What grade did Layla get in chemistry?
qa.a: An A-minus.

qa.q: Why did Sofia feel cheated after Layla's grade?
qa.a: Comparing with Layla, who always seemed one step ahead, made her own best-ever grade feel as if something had been taken from her.

qa.q: What shift in comparison helped Sofia on the metro, and why?
qa.a: Comparing with herself a year ago, when she failed chemistry, which made her B-plus feel like the real progress it was.

qa.q: How might Layla see things, perhaps without knowing Sofia's feelings?
qa.a: Layla may simply be enjoying good grades and holidays, unaware of being the measuring stick for Sofia's mood.

grounding: A teenage girl with a decent situation feels cheated when she compares herself with a classmate one step ahead, and feels better when she compares with her own past.

passage: At the coaching institute, students were split into batches by test score. Ishita, sixteen, made it into Batch B, the second-highest of eight. Her parents were delighted; her cousin in Batch F would have given anything for it. But Ishita's desk looked straight across the corridor into Batch A's room, where Pranav and the others got the senior faculty and the air-conditioning. Every day she felt a sting, as if she'd been robbed. In the canteen she said, "It's so unfair. B gets nothing." Pranav, overhearing, laughed. "You should hear how A talks about last year's toppers." Ishita blinked. She thought of her cousin in Batch F, and of her own score a year ago. The sting didn't vanish, but it shrank.

qa.q: Which batch did Ishita make it into?
qa.a: Batch B, the second-highest of eight.

qa.q: Why did Ishita feel robbed despite being in Batch B?
qa.a: Her desk faced Batch A, so she kept comparing with those one step ahead rather than seeing how well she had done.

qa.q: What helped Ishita's sting shrink, and why?
qa.a: Pranav's remark about Batch A comparing upward, and thinking of her cousin in Batch F and her own score a year ago, which changed whom she was looking at.

qa.q: What does Pranav's reply suggest about how Batch A feels?
qa.a: It suggests Batch A also compares upward and feels behind others, so feeling deprived depends on who you look at.

grounding: A teenage girl in the second-best batch feels cheated by facing the top batch every day, and the feeling shrinks when she looks at others and her own past.

passage:
Dear Irfan Bhai,

You asked why I sounded low on the phone. It's silly. Ammi and Abbu are fine, the shop is doing okay, and we got the roof fixed before the rains. But my friends' families all seem a step ahead. Rehan's dad bought a car, and Adil's family is moving to a bigger flat. When I'm with them I feel like we're struggling, and I come home angry at nothing. Then last week I helped Abbu with the month's accounts. We owe no one. We ate out on Eid. Our roof doesn't leak. If I compare us to five years ago, when we lived in one room, I should be grateful. I suppose it depends on who I'm looking at. Anyway, how is college? Write back.

Abhinav

qa.q: What did the family get fixed before the rains?
qa.a: The roof.

qa.q: How does Abhinav feel when with friends, and why?
qa.a: Abhinav feels the family is struggling and comes home angry, because the friends' families seem a step ahead.

passage: "Another rejection." Nirmala dropped her phone on the flat's only sofa. "That's the eleventh." Tenzin looked up from his laptop. "Sorry, yaar." "Every senior from the batch above got placed in campus week. Every single one. Two years ago companies were queuing up. We get a hiring freeze." "It's not your fault." "Then whose? I did everything right. I topped my section. I was promised this." Tenzin paused. "Who promised?" "Everyone! The brochure, the seniors, my uncle." Her voice cracked. "And now the second-years are getting internships at the same companies that turned me down." "That's rough." "It's more than rough. It's unfair." Tenzin closed the laptop. "The timing is unfair. Want to look at what's actually hiring, together? Tomorrow, not tonight." Nirmala stared at the ceiling. "Tomorrow."

qa.q: Which rejection was this for Nirmala?
qa.a: The eleventh rejection.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's 'I was promised this' reveal about her anger?
qa.a: She feels entitled to the job her seniors got, so the gap between expectation and reality feels like something being withheld.

qa.q: What small step does Tenzin suggest, and why is the timing wise?
qa.a: Looking together at what's actually hiring, tomorrow rather than tonight, so Nirmala can act once the anger has cooled.

qa.q: How does Tenzin seem to see Nirmala's situation?
qa.a: He sees real bad luck in the timing and cares, but gently asks who promised the job, hinting the expectation was never a guarantee.

grounding: A graduate who expected a job like her seniors' feels bitter and entitled, and angrier still as juniors seem to get what she believed was hers.

passage: I'm Farida. When I finished my commerce degree, I was sure I'd walk into a bank job, like the three seniors who had mentored me. They got offers in their final year, and I'd done better than two of them. Then, the year I graduated, the banks froze hiring. I sent out forty applications. I got two interviews and no offers. I remember sitting in Nandini's kitchen, raging. "They owe us. We did what we were told." Nandini said quietly, "Who's they?" I couldn't answer. What made it worse was watching the next batch get internships as things picked up. It felt like the line had moved just as I reached it. It took me months to separate bad luck from the belief that something had been stolen from me.

qa.q: How many applications did Farida send out?
qa.a: Forty applications.

qa.q: Why did it feel worse to Farida when the next batch got internships?
qa.a: It felt like the line had moved just as Farida reached it, making the missed job seem stolen rather than unlucky.

qa.q: What question from Nandini became a turning point, and why?
qa.a: 'Who's they?', because it made Farida see there was no one who owed the job, only bad timing.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt listening to Farida rage in the kitchen?
qa.a: Nandini probably felt concerned and wanted to help Farida see clearly, rather than feed the anger.

grounding: A graduate who expected the jobs their seniors got feels robbed and bitter when a hiring freeze intervenes, and angrier still as the next batch benefits.

passage: Career centre note, 15 January. Written by Binita. Divyansh, twenty-two, came in for the third time this month. He graduated in civil engineering last year, the batch after the one where every student had a site job before exams. His batch met a hiring freeze. He is angry, and says so: "The seniors were no better than me. I earned that job, and it's being kept from me." When he hears that juniors are now landing internships, he goes red and stops listening. I don't doubt his ability. But the anger is making him turn down smaller openings as "beneath what I was promised." Today we listed three firms hiring for project roles and practised one interview. He agreed to apply to two. We meet again on the 29th.

qa.q: How many firms hiring for project roles did they list today?
qa.a: Three firms.

qa.q: What does Divyansh's reaction to juniors getting internships show about how he feels?
qa.a: He goes red and stops listening, showing bitterness that others seem to be getting what he believes he deserved.

qa.q: What did Binita and Divyansh do today, and why is it useful?
qa.a: They listed three firms, practised an interview, and he agreed to apply to two, turning anger into concrete steps.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's anger look to employers offering smaller openings?
qa.a: Employers may see someone who thinks their role is beneath him, missing the capable engineer behind the frustration.

grounding: A career counsellor sees a graduate who expected his seniors' kind of job feel bitter and entitled, especially as juniors get opportunities, and helps him take concrete steps.

passage: Rashmi leaned into the microphone. "Yash, I learned this in my first year as a manager, at twenty-five. The sales team got a new perk: a travel allowance and a quarterly dinner. My support team didn't. Everyone's salary was fair, above the market rate in fact. But within a month my team was sulking. People stopped staying late. One of them said, 'We fix their mistakes, and they get dinners.' I realised it wasn't about money. It was about feeling left behind next to the people one desk away. So I went to management and got the criteria written down: why sales got travel money, which was for actual travel, and what would earn my team the same kind of recognition. I explained it straight, in a team meeting. It didn't fix everything. But the sulking eased once people could see the rules."

qa.q: What new perk did the sales team get?
qa.a: A travel allowance and a quarterly dinner.

qa.q: What did Rashmi realise was really behind the sulking?
qa.a: It wasn't about money; the team felt left behind next to people one desk away who got perks.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do, and why did it ease the resentment?
qa.a: Rashmi got the criteria written down and explained them plainly in a team meeting, so people could see the rules instead of guessing at unfairness.

qa.q: How might the sales team have seen the support team's sulking?
qa.a: The sales team may have been puzzled, seeing the travel allowance as a practical need rather than a reward over others.

grounding: A young manager notices resentment in a fairly paid team when another team gets perks, and eases it with transparent criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: I'm Parul, and I teach in the department Vasudha heads. Last term the school gave new laptops to the senior teachers only. We were all paid on the same scale and nobody was underpaid, but the junior staff went quiet in a way I hadn't seen before. They stopped volunteering for events. Someone left a note on the staffroom board: "Seniors: laptops. Juniors: chalk." Vasudha noticed. I saw her read the note twice and leave it up. At the next meeting she laid out exactly how the laptops had been allotted, by years of service, and admitted the rule had never been explained. Then she got the management to publish when the juniors would get theirs. I can't say what she felt, but her voice was steady. The note came down on its own a week later.

qa.q: What did the note on the staffroom board say?
qa.a: "Seniors: laptops. Juniors: chalk."

qa.q: What does Vasudha reading the note twice and leaving it up suggest?
qa.a: She seemed to take the junior staff's resentment seriously rather than wanting to hide it.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do at the next meeting, and why did it help?
qa.a: She explained how laptops were allotted by years of service, admitted it hadn't been explained, and got a published date for juniors, making the criteria transparent.

qa.q: How might the junior staff feel once the date for their laptops was published?
qa.a: They may feel less left behind, since the rule was now clear and they could see when their turn would come.

grounding: A colleague watches a head of department notice resentment among fairly paid junior staff over a perk and reduce it with clear criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: Week one. Head office announced a festive bonus for the loans team only. Salma, twenty-six and managing the accounts team next door, saw Elizabeth's face harden as she read the email. By Friday the accounts team had stopped chatting with loans at lunch. Week three. The resentment had grown. Elizabeth snapped at a loans officer over a small form. Salma called the regional manager and asked plainly, "What were the criteria?" The answer: the bonus was tied to a loan target accounts had no part in, and accounts had received a pay revision in April that nobody remembered. Week five. Salma put both facts on one slide and explained them at a team meeting, along with the targets that could earn accounts a bonus next year. Elizabeth asked two questions, nodded, and on Friday ate lunch with loans again.

qa.q: Which team got the festive bonus?
qa.a: The loans team.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's hardened face suggest about how she felt reading the email?
qa.a: She felt left out and resentful that the loans team got a bonus while her team did not.

qa.q: What did Salma do in week five, and why did it work?
qa.a: Salma put the bonus criteria and the April pay revision on one slide and explained what could earn accounts a bonus, so the team saw the reasons and a path forward.

qa.q: How might the loans officer have felt when Elizabeth snapped over a small form?
qa.a: The loans officer may have been confused and hurt, not knowing the snap came from resentment about the bonus.

grounding: A young manager notices resentment when another team gets a bonus despite fair pay, and eases it over weeks with transparent criteria and an honest explanation.

passage: The news reached the kasba branch of the cooperative bank before lunch: Ramesh, who had joined on the same day as Jatin, was now assistant branch officer. Jatin smiled and shook his hand, then sat at his counter with his jaw clenched. Ramesh would now sign his leave forms. On the bus home, past the sugarcane fields, Jatin caught the thought going round and round: why him, why not me? He made himself stop. What did he actually have? A steady job four kilometres from his parents, a wife who laughed at his jokes, a scooter fully paid off. What could he control? The officer exam in June, and asking the manager what Ramesh had done that he hadn't. Three years ago he had been jobless, filling in forms at the cyber cafe. By the time he got home, he still wanted the post. He just wasn't angry about it.

qa.q: What post did Ramesh get?
qa.a: Assistant branch officer.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling at his counter after shaking Ramesh's hand?
qa.a: Under the smile he felt envious and resentful, his jaw clenched at the thought of Ramesh signing his leave forms.

qa.q: What questions did Jatin ask himself on the bus, and how did they help?
qa.a: What he actually has and what he can control, plus remembering being jobless three years ago, which let him keep wanting the post without the anger.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel if Jatin had stayed resentful?
qa.a: Ramesh might sense coldness from someone he joined with, making the new role lonelier.

grounding: A young bank clerk fuming at a peer's promotion asks what he has and can control and compares with his own past, keeping ambition without envy.

passage: When the email went round the Toronto design studio announcing that Rania was now senior designer, Kwame felt his face go hot. They'd started the same month. He had stayed later, he told himself. He walked out for coffee to stop himself typing anything. In the queue he did what his older sister always told him: ask three questions. What do I have? A job I like, a portfolio twice as strong as last year's, a mentor who answers my messages. What can I control? My next project, and asking my lead exactly what senior means here. Where was I two years ago? Driving deliveries and sketching on my breaks. By the time his coffee came, the heat had gone. He went back in, stopped at Rania's desk and said, "Congratulations. Can you show me how you pitched the museum brief?"

qa.q: What was Kwame doing two years ago?
qa.a: Driving deliveries and sketching on his breaks.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling when he read the email about Rania?
qa.a: His face went hot; he felt envious and hard done by, telling himself he had stayed later.

qa.q: Which of Kwame's choices shows he kept his ambition without the envy?
qa.a: Going back to congratulate Rania and asking how Rania pitched the museum brief, turning envy into a chance to learn.

qa.q: How might Rania see Kwame's question at Rania's desk?
qa.a: Rania may feel respected and glad that a peer who started the same month is congratulating and learning rather than resenting.

grounding: A young designer fuming at a peer's promotion asks what he has, what he controls and how far he has come, and keeps his ambition without letting envy set the mood.
